generalizedRange: Northern Sumatra, chiefly the Leuser Ecosystem
hook: It lives its whole life in the trees — and the trees are falling.

story.text: A Sumatran orangutan may spend its entire life without touching the ground — almost entirely arboreal, moving on arms that span more than seven feet.
Nine-tenths of its food comes from the canopy: a hundred kinds of ripe fruit, figs and durian above all.
In Sumatra, wild orangutans use tools, working seeds out of hard-shelled fruit.
Every evening, each one weaves a fresh sleeping nest of branches, high in the trees.
They breed more slowly than any other primate: one baby every seven or eight years, dependent on its mother for at least five.
Their stronghold, the Leuser Ecosystem, is the last place on Earth where orangutans, elephants, rhinos, and tigers still live together in the wild.
The threat is the chainsaw's economics: forest logged and converted to oil-palm plantations, roads cutting the survivors into fragments.
Protection is working where it is tried: Sumatra's rescue unit has saved over two hundred orangutans, and two million replanted trees are becoming forest again.
Camera traps at one replanted site recently filmed a wild mother and infant swinging through trees people planted by hand.
To witness the orangutan is to stand with the gardeners of the forest — the seed-carriers the rainforest needs to regrow.

stats.size: 4–4.5 ft tall · males up to 220 lbs
stats.diet: Ripe fruit — figs & durian above all

reproduction.text: No primate breeds more slowly. After eight and a half months of gestation, a single infant stays with its mother for at least five years, nursing for up to seven — a childhood spent learning the map of the forest's fruit.

insight.text: Every night, an orangutan builds a brand-new nest to sleep in — thousands of one-night homes over a lifetime in the canopy.
